::: {.why}
Every null you use for the rest of the year is only as honest as the data-generating process behind it, and a Gaussian random walk fails four of your six criteria.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Generate synthetic return series that reproduce fat tails and volatility clustering to within the tolerances you set on day 42.
- Say which stylized fact your simulator still fails, and what that means for the results you will use it to test.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Build qlib/simulate.py with two generators: a Gaussian random walk, and one with stochastic volatility, where the log variance follows a slow autoregression and the innovations are heavy tailed. Calibrate the second to your own SPY estimates from week 6.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write tests/test_simulate.py asserting the calibrated generator reproduces four of your six stylized facts inside a tolerance you state: kurtosis, absolute-return autocorrelation at lag 1 and lag 20, and the count of four-sigma days. Let the test fail on the leverage effect and the correlation asymmetry, and record in the docstring that it does.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/simulate.py gives the project a null that is not a straw man. Any strategy result from here can be run against synthetic data with the same tails and clustering as the real thing, which is what makes a false-positive rate measurable rather than assumed.
:::

:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your simulator does not reproduce the leverage effect. Name one strategy family whose false positive rate you would therefore be understating.
:::
